The temperature at which a liquid boils and changes into vapor, or gas, is called its boiling point. It can be as high as 212°F (100°C) for water under pressure and as low as -147°F (-39°C).
There are two kinds of boiling points in terms of temperatures at which water becomes vapor: absolute zero and absolute zero. Absolute zero refers to an atom's state when it no longer has any interaction with other atoms or molecules, but rather only exists as a single entity separated from all others by space or time. At this point, there is no heat exchange between them; they do not interact. Absolute zero means that every pair of electrons have no possible combination of electrical charges. This property makes things "cold" and "hot". The three degrees Celsius range above absolute zero is called the freezing point.

Coral reefs are unique ecosystems because they provide us with oxygen and help protect our planet from catastrophic climate change. However, we can’t know exactly how these corals get their nitrogen or carbon dioxide back into the oceans. Some species use dissolved nutrients as a way of fertilizing themselves while others break down organic matter through decomposition and recycling.
One type of marine organism that thrives on this nutrient cycling is a blue-green algae called Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. It lives near the surface of the ocean but does not grow above it. Chlamydomonas reinhardtii produces algal blooms when its cells absorb nutrients like nitrate and phosphate (PO43−) and release them into the water column. The algae then die and sink to the bottom of the sea where they remain until sunlight breaks apart the organic material. As a result, the algae produce a mixture of nitrogen and phosphorous.
Chlamydomonas reinhardtii has evolved over millions of years to live deep inside coral reefs. For decades, scientists have been studying the bacteria that live inside the organisms, which give them energy and allow them to sustain life.
